parts: Please read /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/16_EZ_ASSESSED_ANCHOR_CONTINUATION_20261120.md. I'd like to understand the inverse formula up to K(T)? I'm confused because I thought the approximation got better as height increased, so I'm not sure why the formula is up to that height and not past it.
I’ll read the continuation note and trace \(K(T)\) back to its definition so I can explain which height controls the approximation.
By the way, please put any notes from this conversation in the brainstorm folder, and record chat history in the chat-histories folder

I’ll save the explanation in this investigation’s brainstorm notes and record the conversation in its `chat-histories` folder. I found the cutoff in Note 11 and will check how it relates to the fixed-time, high-zero result.

The \(T=1000\) calculation gives a concrete example. The displayed cutoff rounds down to rank 15, yet a separate calculation counts zero 40 and checks the cubic formula there. I’ll include both numbers in the note, along with the assumptions behind each.

**\(K(T)\) counts zeros from the origin.** Here \(T\) is heat time, \(k\) is a zero’s rank, and \(x_k(T)\) is its height. Your intuition that an approximation improves with height applies to the high-zero formula. The inverse in Note 16 improves as **heat time** increases.

The inverse works by following a cosine phase from \(x=0\). The first zero occurs when the phase reaches \(\pi/2\), the second when it reaches \(3\pi/2\), and the \(k\)-th when it reaches \(q_k=(k-\tfrac12)\pi\). In the interval where the proof tracks those crossings in order, the inverse gives the positions exactly. The **cubic** is the approximation to that inverse. [Note 11, §3](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/11_EZ_GROWING_INVERSE_WINDOW_20261120.md:89)

You can see why the two limits behave differently from the fact that the field averages \(\cos(xU)\) over a range of \(U\). **Raise \(T\)** and the values of \(U\) concentrate more tightly around their mean. The proof can follow more zeros, and even the worst cubic error bound among those zeros tends to zero. **Raise \(x\) at fixed \(T\)** and the same spread in \(U\) produces a larger spread in the angle \(xU\). The cubic error bound grows with rank. The proof keeps a margin inside the exact inverse’s range so it can bound positions and neighboring gaps together. That choice gives \(K(T)\). [Note 11, equations (4)–(6)](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/11_EZ_GROWING_INVERSE_WINDOW_20261120.md:95)

**At \(T=1000\), the displayed cutoff expression rounds down to 15.** Applying the large-time theorem there would also require its finite tests. A separate calculation actually counts **zero 40** at \(x_{40}\approx92.49456\) and finds that the cubic misses it by only \(0.00000639\). So the formula can still give a close answer past the displayed cutoff. [Finite calculation, §6](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:246)

The high-zero result works from the other direction. For example, at \(t=1/2\), Polymath’s formula gets more accurate as height increases, even measured against the shrinking spacing between zeros. The open question in Note 16 is where, at one common time such as \(T=1000\), a bound valid for **every sufficiently high zero** meets a count coming **up from the origin**. [Polymath, §9](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9) · [Note 16, overlap question](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/16_EZ_ASSESSED_ANCHOR_CONTINUATION_20261120.md:35)

[Saved brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/08_EZ_WHY_THE_INVERSE_HAS_A_CUTOFF_20261120.md) · [Chat history](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/chat-histories/0003_2026-11-20T17-34-48Z_explain-the-inverse-formula-cutoff.json)

When brainstorming this sub-investigation, the formula \
\\[\
Y(q)=q+c_1q^3+(3c_1^2+c_2)q^5\
       +(12c_1^3+8c_1c_2+c_3)q^7+\cdots.\
\\]
was presented, where  \\(a x_k(T)=Y(q_k)\\). That was an explicit series for x_k(T), and my understanding was that there was the possibility of resummation. Can you tell me how that is related to the current understanding?
I’ll trace the original series through the resummation formulas and the current proof, including what each one establishes about which zeros it can locate.

The manuscript carries out the resummation. Its “cubic” already includes the \(3c_1^2q^5\) and \(12c_1^3q^7\) terms you quoted. I’ll add that connection to the brainstorm note, including how the terms involving \(c_2,c_3,\ldots\) enter.

Yes. **Your series is the exact inverse used in the current manuscript, and the cubic in Note 16 is a resummation of part of that series.** At a fixed finite \(T\), the mean \(a\) and the coefficients \(c_1,c_2,\ldots\) come from the heated theta source. Wherever the proof establishes convergence and counts the phase crossings, summing the full series gives \(x_k(T)=Y(q_k)/a\) exactly. [Manuscript, counted inverse theorem](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/manuscript/anchors.tex:50)

You can see the resummation in the coefficients you quoted. Collect every term involving \(c_1\) alone:
\[
Y_3(q)=q+c_1q^3+3c_1^2q^5+12c_1^3q^7+\cdots.
\]
This **entire infinite sum** is the solution through zero of \(Y_3-c_1Y_3^3=q\). That is what “cubic” means here. The *equation being inverted* is cubic. Its solution contains arbitrarily high powers of \(q\). For \(h=-c_1>0\), as holds at sufficiently large \(T\), the sum has the closed form
\[
Y_3(q)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3h}}\sinh\!\left(
\frac13\operatorname{arsinh}\!\left(\frac{3\sqrt{3h}}2q\right)\right).
\]
[Founding calculation, §4](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:136)

The remaining terms carry additional information from the source. At order \(q^5\), the cubic already supplies \(3c_1^2\), and the fifth cumulant supplies \(c_2\). At order \(q^7\), the cubic supplies \(12c_1^3\), and the remainder is \(8c_1c_2+c_3\). The founding note also gives an **exact correction series around \(Y_3\)** that restores all those contributions. At \(T=1000\), for the independently counted 40th zero, the cubic’s absolute position error is about \(6.39\times10^{-6}\). Using the degree-seven polynomial you quoted brings it down to \(3.99\times10^{-11}\). [Exact correction series](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:147) · [Fortieth-zero calculation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:246)

**Series order and zero rank answer different questions.** Keeping more terms improves the truncation bound for a given zero inside the proved range. \(K(T)\) tells you how many consecutive zeros receive a common proof of their positions and adjacent-gap errors. A resummed expression can be evaluated at a larger \(q_k\). Using that value to locate a higher zero still requires control of the omitted terms and a count identifying the rank. That is the step Note 16 leaves open. [Note 11, §§3–4](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/11_EZ_GROWING_INVERSE_WINDOW_20261120.md:89)

If you had in mind a **single closed form for the full \(Y\)**, the founding note narrows that possibility. At finite \(T\) it rules out an algebraic formula for \(Y(q)\) as a continuous function of \(q\). A transcendental closed form, or one specific to the discrete values \(q_k\), remains open. [Founding calculation, §7](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:262)

I still don't really understand why this statement "Your intuition that an approximation improves with height applies to the high-zero formula." does not imply that the zeros at large height are approximated better
It does imply that. The high-zero formula gives increasingly accurate positions for sufficiently high zeros in its range. My earlier wording blurred which formula supplied that guarantee.
My confusion is that the discussion has implied that K(T) is the bound beyond which the approximation gets worse, but the intuition says the approximation gets better at larger height
I see where my wording was misleading. \(K(T)\) is the endpoint of a proved range. The error at zero \(K(T)+1\) could be smaller or larger than at zero \(K(T)\).

**\(K(T)\) marks the end of a guarantee.** My earlier wording made it sound like a turning point where the approximation starts getting worse. The paper actually chooses a range where it can bound the cubic’s error for every zero and every neighboring gap at once. \(K(T)\) is the last rank in that range. **The cubic could be more accurate at zero \(K(T)+1\) than at zero \(K(T)\).** The theorem leaves that comparison open. [Note 11, §3](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/11_EZ_GROWING_INVERSE_WINDOW_20261120.md:89)

**Yes, the high-zero formula really does approximate sufficiently high zeros increasingly well.** At heat time \(t=1/2\), for example, every sufficiently high zero lies within **1% of the gap to the next zero** of its predicted position. You can replace 1% with 0.1%, or any smaller positive percentage, by going sufficiently high. [Polymath, §9](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9) · [Note 13, identification of the zero rank](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/13_EZ_CLOCK_RANK_20261120.md:5)

The two formulas predict a position for the same kind of object. If the high-zero formula puts a zero within 1% of a gap, that tells us how close **its prediction** is. To give your resummed cubic the same guarantee there, we would also need to show that **the cubic’s prediction** is close. Where those guarantees meet at \(T=1000\) is the question Note 16 leaves open. [Updated brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/08_EZ_WHY_THE_INVERSE_HAS_A_CUTOFF_20261120.md:50)

Based on the way you are talking about this, I still feel that the research is too focused on numerical experiments, and not enough on understanding the underlying formulas. The intuition is being clouded by the numerics.
I put too much weight on the cutoff. I’ll return to the exact phase that the series inverts and use it to explain what changes at large height. I’ll keep that analysis in the brainstorm folder.

The formulas give a geometric answer. Where the inverse works, successive zeros occur as an angle advances by half a turn. Far out at fixed heat time, that same angle returns to the positive imaginary axis at every zero. This explains why resumming the series and finding a phase that counts the high zeros are different questions.

I gave the cutoff too much attention and buried what your series explains. **What makes the zeros depart from equal spacing?** The formula answers that before any computation.

Near the origin, the field has the exact form
\[
\frac{H_T(x)}{H_T(0)}
=A_T(x)\cos\!\left(ax-\frac{\gamma_3x^3}{6}
                        +\frac{\gamma_5x^5}{120}-\cdots\right),
\qquad A_T(x)>0.
\]
The mean \(a\) sets the basic spacing. The variance and the other even cumulants enter the amplitude. The **asymmetry of the source**, measured first by \(\gamma_3\), shifts the crossings. Your series \(Y\) inverts this angle, and the cubic resummation collects every power of that first asymmetric correction. This gives a geometric prediction. At sufficiently large heat time, the second zero lies slightly *inside* three times the first. A change of overall spacing would preserve that ratio exactly. [Founding derivation, §5](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md:184)

There is an equally concrete reason the high zeros behave differently. Picture the complex integral \(B_T(x)\) moving in the plane. Its real part is \(H_T(x)\), so a zero occurs whenever it meets the imaginary axis. In the range counted by \(Y\), the point turns through successive half-turns. Far out at fixed heat time, integration by parts gives \(B_T(x)=i\Phi(0)/x+O_T(x^{-2})\). **The dominant term sets the direction of the complex integral and contributes exactly zero to its real part.** The point can now cross back and forth over the positive imaginary axis. Each zero returns to the *same angle*. The high-zero formula follows the cancellation of two oscillatory contributions to the real field, whose relative error shrinks with height in its positive-time range. [Half-line endpoint argument](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/04_EZ_HALF_LINE_PHASE_OBSTRUCTION_20261120.md:24) · [Polymath, §9](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9)

That puts \(K(T)\) in perspective. It gives an interval where the first angle provably counts the zeros. The deeper question for resummation is **what limits that inverse branch, and how the same oscillation is encoded once successive zeros return to one angle**. I reorganized the brainstorm note around that question and moved the finite check to the end. [Revised brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/brainstorm/notes/08_EZ_WHY_THE_INVERSE_HAS_A_CUTOFF_20261120.md)
